claim: Social Security raises benefits each December by the rise in the July-September average of the CPI for urban wage earners (CPI-W), so every check paid in a year is priced at the previous summer's level while prices keep moving. Recomputing the raises from CPI-W reproduces the official ones (for example 5.9% for 2022 and 8.7% for 2023). Measured against the very index the law uses, checks paid in 2022 were on average 6.76% short of the summer-2021 price level they were set to match, a loss equal to 0.811 of a monthly check that year and 1.635 of a check over 2021-2023. Over the 40 payment years 1985-2024 the average shortfall was 2.06% a year, adding up to 9.88 monthly checks never recovered; retirees came out ahead in only 4 of those years (when prices fell).

numbers.definition: COLA determined in 2021 (paid from January 2022): round((Q3(2021)/Q3(base)-1)x100, 1), Q3(y) = mean of CWUR0000SA0 (CPI-W, all items, US city average, NSA, monthly) for July, August, September of y; base = most recent earlier year whose computed COLA was > 0, starting the chain with base year 1983 and applying it to every year 1984..2023 (a year whose computed value is <= 0 gets no COLA and leaves the base unchanged).
Same as cola_2021_pct for the year 2022 (paid from January 2023).

Mean over the 12 months m of 2022 of (1 - Q3(b)/CPIW(m)) x 100, where b = base year in force for benefits paid in 2022 (the latest year <= 2021 with a positive computed COLA, here 2021) and CPIW(m) = CWUR0000SA0 for month m.
Sum over the 12 months of 2022 of (1 - Q3(b)/CPIW(m)), i.e. purchasing power missing relative to a check indexed to the base-quarter price level, in units of one monthly check.
Sum of the monthly shortfalls (1 - Q3(b_Y)/CPIW(m)) over all months of payment years 2021, 2022 and 2023, where b_Y = latest year <= Y-1 with a positive computed COLA.
Sum of the monthly shortfalls (1 - Q3(b_Y)/CPIW(m)) over all 480 months of payment years Y = 1985..2024 (negative months, when prices were below the base level, are included and offset).
Number of payment years Y in 1985..2024 whose 12-month sum of shortfalls is negative.

assumptions: The benefit paid in each month of year Y is indexed exactly to the base-quarter CPI-W level (Q3 of the last year with a COLA); rounding of COLAs to 0.1% and of benefits to the dime is ignored in the shortfall.
The December increase is first received in the January check, so a raise determined in year y applies to checks paid in year y+1.
CPI-W is used both for the COLA and as the yardstick, so the result measures only the timing lag, not any difference between CPI-W and retirees' actual spending.
The wage-index alternative in 415(i)(1)(C)(ii) (low trust-fund ratio) never applied in these years; the CPI rule is used throughout. The COLA chain starts from the 1983 base quarter.

series.provider: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

provisions.quote: the term "base quarter" means (i) the calendar quarter ending on September 30 in each year after 1982

the term "CPI increase percentage", with respect to a base quarter or cost-of-living computation quarter in any calendar year, means the percentage (rounded to the nearest one-tenth of 1 percent) by which the Consumer Price Index for that quarter (as prepared by the Department of Labor) exceeds such index for the most recent prior calendar quarter which was a base quarter under subparagraph (A)(ii) or, if later, the most recent cost-of-living computation quarter under subparagraph (B);
the Consumer Price Index for a base quarter, a cost-of-living computation quarter, or any other calendar quarter shall be the arithmetical mean of such index for the 3 months in such quarter.
